title: Modular tests rule

short.lead: Proposal: house rules will require every test to be a self-contained module that runs alone or chained, refuse new tests that are not, and list old ones that are not; you pick how strict and how far the first build goes.
short.hint: Tap a step to see it.
items: A test is a module, not a slice of one big run

A new rule section and a detail file. A test names its module, runs alone with one command, needs no other module's leftovers, and chains with others through one runner. Only a test that is meant to check the whole system may run every check.

items.alt: Today a change to one tool runs all of verify_tools.py. After: only the module you changed.
items.caption: Today a change to one tool runs all of verify_tools.py. After: only the module you changed.

items: New tests are refused unless they follow it
A hook checks each test file Claude writes or edits and refuses one with no module name or no stand-alone command, saying how to fix it.

items.alt: The gate: a test file with a module is saved, one without is refused with the fix.
items.caption: The gate: a test file with a module is saved, one without is refused with the fix.

items: Old tests are named in a docs file, then work goes on
A command lists every existing test that is not modular and writes the list to the state tier of the docs. Work continues. Inside a refactor, listed tests must be converted first.

items.alt: The audit writes the list; a refactor turns the list into work.
items.caption: The audit writes the list; a refactor turns the list into work.

items: One command converts an old test
A skill and a slash command, `/house-rules:modular-tests audit` and `/house-rules:modular-tests convert <path>`, split one test file into modules without changing what it checks.
I add one line to the decisions log.
Pick an option for each of the three questions under Your choices, then tap Copy my reply and send it.

new
Rule section and detail file
Tests are modules
A section in `rules/house-rules.md`, a detail file, a `checks.json` entry, and a `verify.py` case so the rule is enforced and not just written.
`green-suite.md` already says to run only touched parts.
A rule that makes that mandatory for every test.
Every future test I write is a module.
new
Test-module hook
Refuses a non-modular test at write time
Checks files that look like tests (`test_*`, `*_test.*`, `verify*.py`). It reads a module header and a stand-alone command, and refuses with the fix. A file declared end-to-end passes.
Nothing checks test shape today.
One new check in `hook.py`, with its own cases.
A refusal appears once, naming what to add.
new
modular-tests skill and command
Audit and convert in one command
`audit` writes `docs/3-state/non-modular-tests.md`. `convert <path>` splits a file into modules and proves the old and new runs give the same results.
Commands exist for docs, labels and modes only.
A skill, a command and one script.
You type one line to convert a file.
choices: first
How strict is the refusal?
A
Refuse at write time (suggested)
The hook refuses a test file with no module header or no stand-alone command, which matches your wording that new tests are refused.
B
Refuse at write time and fail the pull request's automatic checks too
Same hook, plus a `verify.py` check that fails a pull request containing a non-modular test. Stricter, and catches edits made outside Claude.
C
Warn only
The hook reminds but does not refuse. Not what you asked for; listed for completeness.
A matches the words you used, and the pull-request check can be added later without redoing anything.
second
What counts as a refactor, the point at which listed tests must be converted?
A
A line you type: `refactor on` (suggested)
Works like the `pages off` and `builders off` switches: `refactor off` ends it. It is explicit, so the hook never guesses.
B
Any issue labelled `refactor`
Needs no typing, but depends on every refactor being labelled first.
C
I decide and say so
No setup, but nothing checks my judgment.
A is the only option the hook can check without guessing.
third
How far does the first build go?
A
Rule, hook, skill, command, audit; then convert verify_tools.py as the proof (suggested)
Shows the whole loop working on one real file. The two offshoot suites become one issue each.
B
All of the above, plus convert every suite now
Biggest change, with the most risk. Needs one issue per suite: verify_tools.py, agent-router and prompt-workshop, plus the rule work, so four issues.
C
Rule, hook, skill, command, audit only; convert nothing yet
Smallest. The audit list is the only evidence the conversion works.
A proves the conversion on real code without converting three suites at once (verify_tools.py, agent-router and prompt-workshop).

wrapup.summary: This proposal adds a modular-tests rule, a hook that refuses non-modular new tests, an audit that lists old ones, and a skill and command to convert them.
wrapup.changing: The rules file, one hook check, one new skill and command, a state-tier doc listing non-modular tests, and, if you pick option A under the third choice, tools/verify_tools.py split into modules.
wrapup.blocking: Your three choices: how strict the refusal is, what counts as a refactor, and how far the first build goes. I also need the repository name for Plunderspell, your other project, as owner/repo, because I do not have it. The rule is global, so it applies to Plunderspell's tests too, but converting them is an issue in that repository.
